notes:
Task and constraints: Decode a string whose bracketed substrings are repeated by a preceding positive integer.
Idea: Push input characters onto a stack and expand a bracketed segment when its closing bracket arrives.
Technique and why it applies: At a closing bracket, the code pops the encoded substring back to the opening bracket, collects preceding digits, and pushes the repeated string. Nested expressions work because an inner expansion is pushed back for outer expansion.
Invariant: Before a closing bracket, the stack holds the unprocessed prefix and any completed inner expansions.
Edge cases: Multi-digit repeat counts are collected in reverse-pop order. The encoding is assumed valid; a closing bracket without an opening bracket would access an invalid stack position.
Complexity: Stack processing is O(n) excluding output construction, but repeated string prepending while popping can be quadratic in segment length. Storage is O(n) plus decoded output, which can be much larger than the encoded input.

Task and constraints: Expand a valid encoded string with repeat counts and nested bracket expressions.
Idea: Maintain the current decoded character list plus stacks for parent strings and repeat counts.
Technique and why it applies: On an opening bracket, save the current prefix and multiplier; on a closing bracket, repeat the current segment and extend the saved prefix. Digit accumulation supports multi-digit counts.
Invariant: curr is the decoded content of the currently open level, while strs and nums hold its parent context and repeat count.
Edge cases: Plain alphabetic characters append directly. The code assumes the input grammar uses letters, digits, and brackets as expected; other characters are ignored.
Complexity: Processing costs O(n + L), where L is decoded output length; list repetition and extension create output proportional to L. Auxiliary stack space is O(n) in nesting depth plus output storage. The author labels are broadly consistent if n includes output size.

Task and constraints: Find the longest substring in which every character that appears occurs at least k times.
Idea: Count frequencies, identify characters occurring fewer than k times, and split the string at those characters.
Technique and why it applies: A character with total frequency below k cannot belong to any valid substring, so each such position is a separator. The function recursively evaluates each resulting segment and takes the maximum length.
Invariant: Every recursive segment excludes the low-frequency separator characters identified for that call.
Edge cases: Empty strings return zero; if no character is under-frequency, the whole segment is valid.
Complexity: Each call scans and slices its segment, and recursion can repeat work across levels; worst-case time can reach O(n²) with slicing and repeated scans. Space can be O(n) for substrings and recursion, aside from Counter storage.

Task and constraints: Return the longest substring where each character in that substring occurs at least k times.
Idea: Count letters in a range, skip characters whose frequency is too small, and recurse on contiguous ranges between them.
Technique and why it applies: Any character appearing fewer than k times in a range cannot appear in a valid answer for that range, so it splits the problem. The helper uses a fixed 26-element array for lowercase letters.
Invariant: Each recursive call considers only its [start,end) range, and max_len stores the best valid child result seen.
Edge cases: Empty ranges return zero through the loop. The code assumes lowercase English input because it indexes counts by ord(c)-ord('a').
Complexity: A call counts its range and may recurse on disjoint subranges; with a fixed alphabet the intended bound is O(26n), or O(n) for a constant alphabet. The count array is O(1), with recursion stack potentially O(n).

Task and constraints: Find the maximum rotation function F(k), the sum of each rotated value multiplied by its index.
Idea: Compute F(0) and the sum of all values, then update the function in constant time for each rotation.
Technique and why it applies: Rotating moves the last value from index n-1 to index 0; the total sum contributes once to the change, while that moved value loses n times its value.
Invariant: cur is the function value for the current rotation and ans is the maximum value encountered so far.
Edge cases: An empty nums list returns zero because both loops are skipped. The recurrence assumes ordinary integer arithmetic and a list of values.
Complexity: The initial pass and rotation pass each scan the array once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Maximize the rotation function across all clockwise rotations of the array.
Idea: Start with the weighted sum and total sum, then derive each next rotation from the previous one.
Technique and why it applies: The recurrence adds the sum of all elements and subtracts n times the element moved from the end to the front. The code evaluates n rotations, updating the maximum after each.
Invariant: fi represents the current rotation score; result holds the largest score found.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero, since the loops and initial weighted sum are empty. The last loop iteration evaluates a full cycle back to the original arrangement, which does not change the maximum.
Complexity: Computing the sum and initial score plus n recurrence updates takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, matching the labels.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum operations to reduce positive integer n to one, halving even values or incrementing/decrementing odd values.
Idea: Use memoized recursion to compare both possible operations for odd values and take the cheaper path.
Technique and why it applies: Even values have one legal next state; odd values branch to num-1 and num+1. dp caches completed results so repeated states are not recomputed.
Invariant: dfs(num) returns the minimum operation count from num to one, and dp stores that value once calculated.
Edge cases: n=1 returns zero. Very large values may reach deep recursion or hit Python's recursion limit, especially along recursive increment/halving paths.
Complexity: The number of memoized integer states is bounded by the states visited along these transitions, typically logarithmically many nearby values; each state does constant work. Memo and recursion storage scale with visited states.

Task and constraints: Evaluate division queries from equations such as A/B=value, returning -1 when variables are disconnected or unknown.
Idea: Build a bidirectional weighted graph and search for a path whose edge ratios multiply to the query ratio.
Technique and why it applies: Each equation adds A-to-B with value and B-to-A with reciprocal. DFS accumulates the product along a path and uses visited to avoid cycles.
Invariant: product is the ratio from the DFS start to the current node along the selected path.
Edge cases: Unknown variables return -1 through the graph-membership guard, which refers to the current query variables captured from the surrounding loop. The code assumes nonzero equation values because it computes 1/v.
Complexity: Graph construction is O(E); each query may traverse O(V+E), so total is O(E+Q(V+E)) time and O(V+E) graph storage, plus visited sets and answers.

Task and constraints: Return the nth digit in the infinite sequence formed by concatenating positive integers in order.
Idea: Find the digit-width block containing n, calculate the target number and digit position, then extract that digit.
Technique and why it applies: Each width-p block contains 9·10^(p-1) numbers and therefore a known number of digits. After subtracting earlier blocks, integer division locates the number and the remainder identifies the digit from the right.
Invariant: low is the first number in the current width block and sum_ counts digits in all preceding blocks.
Edge cases: The problem uses positive n. The extraction loop has no explicit final fallback, but valid arithmetic should return when the target digit is reached.
Complexity: The block loop iterates O(log n) times, and digit extraction scans at most O(log n) digits; auxiliary space is O(1).

Task and constraints: List all watch times whose hour and minute binary representations contain exactly turnedOn set bits.
Idea: Enumerate all 12 valid hours and 60 valid minutes, count their one-bits, and retain matching pairs.
Technique and why it applies: The watch has only 720 hour-minute combinations, so exhaustive enumeration is small and directly checks the required LED count. Formatting with :02d keeps minutes two digits.
Invariant: output contains exactly the qualifying combinations among pairs examined so far.
Edge cases: turnedOn=0 yields 0:00. If turnedOn exceeds the total possible 10 LEDs, the result is empty.
Complexity: There are 12×60 fixed combinations and each bit count examines a fixed-width value, so time is O(1) under the watch constraints. Output space is O(1) under the same fixed bound.

Task and constraints: Return every valid binary-watch time with exactly num LEDs turned on.
Idea: Enumerate all legal hour and minute pairs and compare their bit counts with num.
Technique and why it applies: bit_count repeatedly clears the lowest set bit using bits &= bits-1, counting one iteration per set bit. The list comprehension keeps only combinations whose hour and minute counts sum to num.
Invariant: Each emitted string corresponds to a distinct legal time with the required total number of set bits.
Edge cases: Hours range from 0 to 11 and minutes from 0 to 59; formatting ensures minutes have two digits. Impossible LED counts naturally produce an empty list.
Complexity: Enumeration is 720 fixed cases and bit counting is bounded by small fixed-width integers, so O(1) time under problem constraints. Output space is also bounded by the finite watch.

Task and constraints: Remove k digits from a non-negative decimal string to obtain the smallest possible number.
Idea: Use a monotonic stack of digits and original indices, marking digits removed when a later smaller digit appears.
Technique and why it applies: When the current digit is smaller than the stack top, deleting that larger earlier digit improves the prefix. deleteindexes rebuilds the number without marked positions and strips leading zeros by converting to int in one branch.
Invariant: The stack retains digits not yet marked for deletion, with a nondecreasing tendency where removals have been performed.
Edge cases: len(s)==k returns '0'. The post-loop slicing arithmetic is difficult to verify and can remove an incorrect number of trailing digits; converting through int also normalizes leading zeros.
Complexity: Each digit is pushed and popped at most once, but rebuilding through list comprehensions can add O(n) work. The stack, deletion map, and rebuilt string use O(n) space. Correctness needs targeted tests for k removals not all triggered during scanning.

Task and constraints: Remove k digits from num to make the resulting non-negative integer as small as possible.
Idea: Maintain a monotonic increasing digit stack and remove larger previous digits whenever a smaller digit arrives and deletions remain.
Technique and why it applies: A smaller digit placed earlier reduces the number more significantly than keeping a larger prefix digit. After scanning, join the stack, strip leading zeros, and remove any remaining k digits from the end.
Invariant: result is the smallest retained prefix achievable with the deletions used so far.
Edge cases: The final slice removes k trailing digits only when k remains positive; the fallback '0' handles an empty result.
Complexity: Each digit is appended once and popped at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) stack/output space, consistent with the author labels.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a frog can reach the final stone using jumps whose lengths change by at most one from the previous jump.
Idea: For each stone position, store the jump lengths that can land there and propagate the next three possible lengths.
Technique and why it applies: From a stone reached with jump j, the next jump may be j-1, j, or j+1; positive jumps are added only when the destination is an existing stone.
Invariant: last_jump_units[s] contains jump sizes that can reach stone s under the allowed transitions.
Edge cases: The code immediately reads stones[1], so lists shorter than two stones are not handled. It assumes the first jump must be one and that stones contains unique sorted positions.
Complexity: Up to O(n) jump sizes can be stored at each of n stones, giving O(n²) time and O(n²) space in the worst case, matching the author labels.

Task and constraints: Convert an integer to lowercase hexadecimal, using two's-complement representation for negatives.
Idea: Repeatedly extract the low four bits, map them to a hexadecimal character, then reverse the collected digits.
Technique and why it applies: num & 15 obtains the lowest nibble and right shift advances to the next nibble. Limiting output to eight digits matches a 32-bit two's-complement representation for negative values.
Invariant: result contains the low-order hexadecimal digits extracted so far, in reverse order.
Edge cases: Zero returns '0'. Negative integers terminate after eight digits because Python's right shift preserves the sign bit; the cap prevents an infinite loop.
Complexity: At most eight iterations execute under the 32-bit representation rule, so time and auxiliary space are O(1). The author O(log n) time label is not tight for this capped implementation.

Task and constraints: Reconstruct a queue so each person has exactly k people of at least their height ahead of them.
Idea: Sort people by height and place each person into the first empty slot reached after counting the required number of qualifying positions.
Technique and why it applies: Shorter people are placed first; while scanning positions, empty slots and already placed people at least as tall as the current person affect the counter.
Invariant: After each placement, the algorithm intends to satisfy the current person's k condition while preserving earlier placements.
Edge cases: ans = [[]] * n initially aliases the same empty list object in every slot, though assigning a new list to a slot breaks that alias for that position. pop(0) repeatedly shifts the input list.
Complexity: Sorting and repeated front pops plus slot scans make the algorithm O(n²) overall, with O(n) queue storage. The greedy placement order and counter should be tested carefully against equal-height cases.

Task and constraints: Calculate how much water a 2D height map traps after rain, with water able to escape at the boundary.
Idea: Seed a min-heap with all boundary cells and expand inward from the lowest current boundary.
Technique and why it applies: When a cell at effective boundary height h reaches an unvisited neighbor, trapped water is max(0, h-neighborHeight). The neighbor is pushed with effective height max(h, neighborHeight), representing the lowest wall level known along that path.
Invariant: Every visited cell has been incorporated into the boundary frontier at its effective escape height.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty rectangular map. Boundary cells are marked visited before processing so each cell is added once.
Complexity: Each cell is pushed and popped once with heap operations O(log(mn)), giving O(mn log(mn)) time and O(mn) space for m×n cells.

Task and constraints: Return the trapped water volume in an m-by-n elevation map.
Idea: Use a min-heap flood fill starting from every boundary cell, marking cells visited when they enter the heap.
Technique and why it applies: The lowest boundary height is processed first. For each unvisited neighbor, the code adds the positive difference between the current effective height and terrain height, then pushes the neighbor at the larger of those heights.
Invariant: The heap represents the current lowest reachable boundary frontier, and visited prevents processing a cell twice.
Edge cases: Empty row or column dimensions return zero. A one-row or one-column map seeds boundary cells redundantly, but visited flags prevent re-adding them during expansion.
Complexity: Every cell enters the heap at most once, giving O(mn log(mn)) time and O(mn) space. The author labels were not supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum length of a palindrome constructible from the characters of a case-sensitive string.
Idea: Count each character and use all pairs, with at most one leftover odd occurrence in the center.
Technique and why it applies: An even count contributes fully; an odd count contributes count-1 as pairs and makes a center character available. Only one center can be used, tracked by plus1.
Invariant: ans contains the number of characters used in pairs, and plus1 records whether any odd count can supply a center.
Edge cases: A string with no characters returns zero. Uppercase and lowercase letters are separate dictionary keys, consistent with case sensitivity.
Complexity: Counting and processing frequencies take O(n) expected time and O(u) auxiliary space for u distinct characters.

Task and constraints: Return the longest palindrome length that can be assembled from a case-sensitive string's characters.
Idea: Count the number of characters with odd frequencies, then subtract their excess odd characters from the full length.
Technique and why it applies: Every odd frequency must lose one character to become pairable, except that one odd character may be placed at the center. Thus the result is len(s)-odds plus one if any odd frequency exists.
Invariant: odds counts distinct characters whose frequency is odd, not the total number of odd-occurring characters.
Edge cases: If all frequencies are even, no center bonus is added. Counter treats uppercase and lowercase separately.
Complexity: Counter counts the string in O(n) expected time and uses O(u) space for u distinct characters.
